opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we get a lot. The short answer is that even if a hyperscaler or a neocloud is ultimately putting our cards and trays into their own racks, inference performance today isn't determined at the chip level anymore. It's determined at the system level.

When you're serving large models, especially with long contexts, agentic workflows, and lots of concurrent users, the bottlenecks show up in places that have nothing to do with how fast an individual piece of silicon can do matrix math. They show up in how memory is shared across devices, how you scale out across cards and trays, how the interconnect behaves under load, how you manage power and cooling at density, and how the software stack orchestrates all of that. If you only understand the chip, you end up building something that looks great on a spec sheet and then disappoints when it's deployed at scale.

So for us, building rack-scale expertise is really about designing with the end deployment in mind. We need to know what a customer's rack looks like: the power envelope per rack, the thermal constraints, the networking fabric, how many accelerators they want per node, how they're going to scale to many nodes. That shapes decisions we make all the way down to the silicon and the memory architecture. It also shapes how we build our software, because the customer doesn't want to be handed a card and told, "Good luck." They want a solution that drops into their environment and delivers predictable tokens per second, per watt, per dollar.

There's also a practical reality. The largest hyperscalers have deep infrastructure teams, and they'll absolutely do their own integration. But even they want a partner who speaks their language at the rack level, who can say, "Here's the reference design, here's how it behaves at full load, here's the performance you should expect when you scale out." And the long tail of neoclouds and enterprises, frankly, often wants us to go further and help them with the whole rack, or something close to a turnkey system.

So it's not that we want to be in the business of competing with our customers on building racks. It's that if we want our technology to actually win in production inference, we have to understand and optimize for the system it lives in. The rack is really the new unit of compute, and if you don't think at that level, you're going to leave a lot of performance and efficiency on the table.

r001.rationale: The response says hyperscalers and neoclouds integrate products into their own racks, yet still want a partner with rack-level expertise and reference designs.

r002.rationale: It describes understanding and optimizing the rack system for deployment, but does not say d-Matrix needs that expertise to troubleshoot problems in customer racks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a fair question, and honestly it's one we debated internally for a while. The short version is: the card and the tray are not the product anymore. The rack is the product. Even if the customer physically owns the rack and puts our trays in it, the thing they're actually buying is tokens per second per dollar per watt at the rack level, and you can't deliver that if you only think about your slice of it.

Let me give you a few concrete reasons.

The first is that inference, especially at the scale these folks are running it, is a distributed problem. A single card doesn't serve a frontier model. You're sharding the model across many chips, and now the interconnect, the topology, how traffic moves between trays, how you handle the KV cache across the fabric, all of that becomes part of the performance equation. If we just threw a card over the wall and said "good luck," the customer would end up with a system that performs nothing like our benchmarks. So we had to understand the full fabric to even make honest claims about what the silicon does.

The second is power and thermals. Hyperscalers are now building for 100 kilowatts, 150 kilowatts a rack and climbing. Our whole thesis is efficiency, that in-memory compute lets you do more work per watt. But that advantage can get eaten alive if the rack-level cooling, the power delivery, the airflow isn't designed around it. We've seen cases where the chip is great and the integration undoes the benefit. So we need to be in the room for those decisions, or at minimum ship a reference design that reflects what we've learned.

The third one, and this is maybe the less obvious one, is that the big customers actually want this from us. People assume hyperscalers want a bare component so they can do everything themselves. In practice, their platform teams are stretched thin. They've got dozens of accelerators competing for attention. The vendor who shows up with a validated rack-scale reference, with the networking, the software stack, the serving layer all tuned together, that vendor gets deployed faster. The one who shows up with a card and a datasheet waits in line. Time to deployment is the actual currency right now.

And then there's the neocloud piece. The neoclouds are often not as deep on infrastructure engineering as a Google or a Microsoft. For them, rack-scale expertise isn't a nice-to-have, it's how they get to revenue. So having that capability lets us serve both ends of the market with one design philosophy.

I'd add one last thing. Building rack-scale knowledge is also how we learn what to put in the next chip. The feedback loop from a real deployment, what bottlenecks show up, where memory bandwidth actually binds, where the software falls over, that's where the next generation comes from. If we outsourced all of that understanding to our customers, we'd be designing silicon blind. So even if we never sold a single rack ourselves, we'd still need to be experts at it.

r001.rationale: The response says hyperscalers value vendors who provide a validated rack-scale design because their platform teams are stretched thin, even though customers physically own and assemble the racks.

r002.rationale: It explains that understanding the full fabric lets d-Matrix identify why deployed systems underperform benchmarks, and that deployment feedback reveals bottlenecks in memory bandwidth and software.

astra-6.text:
Because the rack is really becoming the unit of compute for inference. A card can have great performance, but what matters to the customer is how the whole system performs when you connect those cards together and run a model across them. That means thinking about networking, power, cooling, and the software that coordinates everything.

The hyperscalers and the large neoclouds absolutely have their own rack expertise. We need to be able to work with those teams and understand their constraints, so that what we deliver fits into their infrastructure and delivers the performance they expect. You can’t optimize the chip in isolation and assume everything else will take care of itself.

So having rack-scale expertise doesn’t necessarily mean we have to build and deliver every rack ourselves. It means we take responsibility for understanding how our technology works at that scale, and we can give our partners a system architecture they can actually deploy.

r001.rationale: The candidate says hyperscalers and neoclouds have their own rack expertise, but d-Matrix must understand their constraints and how its technology works at rack scale so its products fit their infrastructure.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses system performance, integration, and architecture, but does not say d-Matrix needs this expertise to troubleshoot deployment problems in customer racks.

sol-6.1.text:
Because our customers ultimately care about what the whole rack delivers, not just what an individual card delivers. They may deploy our trays and cards in their own racks, but we still need to understand how those systems come together—the networking, the power, the cooling, and the software that coordinates inference across them.

You can have a very fast chip and still leave a lot of performance on the table if the system around it isn’t balanced. So rack-scale expertise helps us design our part of that system properly and work with customers to make sure they get the throughput, latency, and economics they’re looking for. It doesn’t mean we have to build everybody’s rack. It means we have to understand the environment our technology operates in.

r001.rationale: It says customers deploy the trays and cards in their own racks but still care about whole-rack performance, so d-Matrix needs to understand how the rack’s systems work together.

r002.rationale: It discusses balancing the system and helping customers meet performance goals, but does not explain that in-house rack-scale expertise is needed to troubleshoot deployment problems.
